faq.a: Yes, if you use it as a tutor: ask for explanations, small exercises and feedback, then type and run the code yourself. Copying large answers without understanding them slows real learning.

faq.q: Is AI-generated code always correct?
faq.a: No. It can contain bugs, outdated methods or insecure patterns. Run the code, test edge cases, read what each line does and consult official documentation for anything important. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: What should I ask when my code throws an error?
faq.a: Share the exact error message, the relevant code, what you expected and what happened. Ask it to explain the cause first, then suggest a fix, so you understand the problem.

faq.q: Which programming language should I start with?
faq.a: Pick one that fits your goal, such as a beginner-friendly language for scripts, websites or data. Ask an assistant to compare options for your goal, then commit to one for a few months.

title: AI Voice and Transcription Workflow for Interviews and Lectures
excerpt: Record, transcribe, clean and summarise audio with AI. A practical workflow with consent tips, recording advice, cleanup prompts and accuracy checks.
seo_title: AI Voice and Transcription Workflow Guide
seo_description: A step-by-step workflow for turning audio into clean text with AI: recording tips, consent, transcription cleanup, summaries, quotes and accuracy checks.
content:
The best AI transcription workflow starts before you press record: get permission, capture clean audio, transcribe, correct the names and numbers by ear, and only then ask an assistant to summarise or extract. Each stage guards against a different kind of error, and skipping the early ones makes the later ones much harder.

## Stage 1: Get consent and know the rules

Recording people is regulated in many places, and rules differ between countries, regions, schools and workplaces. Before you record anyone:

- Tell them you want to record and why.
- Explain who will hear or read it and how long you will keep it.
- Get their agreement, ideally in writing or on the recording itself.
- Follow your school's or employer's policy, especially for lectures, patient or client conversations and confidential meetings.

If you are unsure, do not record. Take notes instead.

### Stage 2: Capture clean audio

Transcription quality depends heavily on the recording. Small steps give large gains:

- Choose a quiet room, and close windows and doors.
- Put the microphone near the speaker, not across the room.
- Do a ten-second test and listen back.
- Ask people to speak one at a time.
- Say unusual names and terms clearly, and spell them once at the start.
- Keep the file in a standard format and back it up.

For interviews, a plain headset or a small external microphone usually beats the built-in microphone of a laptop in a noisy cafe.

## Stage 3: Transcribe

Use a transcription tool that your school or workplace allows and whose data handling you have read about on its official site. Some process audio on remote servers, and policies on storage and training vary. If the content is sensitive, check that the tool fits your obligations or transcribe locally with a tool you trust.

Choose options like speaker labels and timestamps if available. Timestamps let you jump to the exact moment later to confirm a quote.

### Stage 4: Correct the transcript by ear

Never skip this step. Play the audio at a comfortable speed while reading, and fix:

- Proper names, places and organisations.
- Numbers, dates and units.
- Technical terms and acronyms.
- Places where speakers interrupted each other.
- Anything marked as inaudible, which you may be able to resolve by listening again.

Mark uncertain parts with a symbol like [?] instead of guessing.

## Stage 5: Clean the text with an assistant

Once the transcript is accurate, use a chat assistant to tidy it for reading. Be explicit that you want formatting changes, not new content:

```
Clean this transcript for readability. Remove filler words like "um" and "you know", fix obvious punctuation,
and split into paragraphs by topic. Keep the speaker labels. Do not change meaning, add words, or fix facts.
If a sentence is unclear, leave it as is and mark it with [unclear].
```

Keep the original raw transcript saved, so you can always return to what was actually said.

### Stage 6: Summarise and extract

Different goals need different prompts.

**For a lecture:**

```
From this lecture transcript, create: (1) an outline with headings in the order covered,
(2) a list of definitions, (3) any examples given, (4) questions the lecturer posed,
(5) five review questions I can use to test myself. Use only what is in the transcript.
```

**For an interview:**

```
List the main themes. For each, give two short verbatim quotes with the timestamp.
Flag any statements that contradict each other. Do not paraphrase inside quotation marks.
```

Quotes are risky. Always check them against the audio before publishing, and make sure you represent the speaker fairly and in context.

## Stage 7: Store and protect

Audio and transcripts can contain personal data. Store them in a secure, access-controlled place, delete what you no longer need, and share only the minimum. For research, follow your ethics approval and data management plan. Remove names and identifying details when you share excerpts.

### Voice for writing, not just recording

Dictation is another useful workflow. Speak a rough first draft of an email, a blog outline or a reflection, transcribe it, then ask an assistant to organise it into sections. Many people think more freely out loud than at a keyboard. Treat the output as raw material, and edit it in your own voice.

## Accessibility benefits

Transcripts help people who are deaf or hard of hearing, those studying in a second language, and anyone who prefers reading. If you publish audio or video, provide a corrected transcript. An uncorrected machine transcript can mislead, so review it first.

### A worked example: a thirty-minute interview

You record a thirty-minute interview with a local shop owner for a school project, with written permission. You use a quiet back room and a headset microphone. After transcribing, you play the recording and correct three misspelled business names and one price. You save the corrected raw transcript, then ask the assistant for themes with timestamps. It returns four themes. You listen to each quoted moment to confirm the wording, trim one quote that lost its context, and ask the shop owner to review the final excerpts before you use them.

The whole process takes longer than pressing a button, but the result is accurate, fair and ready to cite. The assistant did the sorting; you did the verifying.

## Handling multiple languages and accents

If speakers switch languages or have strong regional accents, accuracy often drops. Tell the tool which language to expect where it allows that, and check names carefully. For mixed-language content, consider transcribing sections separately. Always review such transcripts with extra care, since errors can change meaning.

## Common mistakes

- **Recording without permission.**
- **Poor audio.** Software cannot rescue a noisy room.
- **Trusting the transcript blindly.** Names and numbers are often wrong.
- **Letting AI fix content while cleaning.** Ask only for formatting changes.
- **Quoting from a summary** rather than the verified transcript.
- **Keeping sensitive audio indefinitely.**

## Next steps

Find note-taking templates in [/prompts/category/productivity](/prompts/category/productivity), organise study sessions with the [study planner](/study-planner), and review more tools in [/ai-tools](/ai-tools).

faq.a: Accuracy varies with audio quality, accents, background noise and subject vocabulary. Treat every transcript as a draft, and check names, numbers and technical terms against the recording. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: Do I need consent to record and transcribe someone?
faq.a: Rules differ by country, workplace and situation. Ask permission, explain how the recording will be used, and follow local law and organisational policy, especially for interviews and private conversations. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: How can I improve my transcription results?
faq.a: Record in a quiet room, place the microphone close to the speaker, avoid people talking over each other, and say names and unusual terms clearly. Good audio matters more than any software setting.

faq.q: Can AI summarise a lecture transcript?
faq.a: Yes, it can produce outlines and key points. Because lectures are dense, ask for section-by-section summaries, compare with your own notes, and check anything you plan to cite or memorise.

title: AI Automation Basics: Triggers, Actions and Your First Workflow
excerpt: New to automation? Learn the trigger-action idea, pick a small repetitive task, design the steps on paper and add an AI step safely with a human check.
seo_title: AI Automation Basics: Triggers and Actions
seo_description: Learn how automation works with simple triggers and actions, how to choose a first task, add an AI step safely, and test and monitor your workflow.
content:
Every automation, however fancy, is built from the same idea: when something happens (a trigger), do something in response (an action). AI adds an optional middle step that reads, classifies or drafts. If you start with one small, low-risk task, map it on paper, and keep a human approval step until it proves reliable, you can build useful workflows without writing code.

## The trigger-action model

Think of a simple rule: "When a new form response arrives, add a row to my spreadsheet." The trigger is the new response. The action is the new row. Almost all automation tools, from simple no-code services to advanced platforms, use this pattern. Their interfaces differ and change, so look at each tool's official help rather than relying on screenshots in old tutorials.

A third piece appears often: **conditions**. "If the response mentions a refund, notify me; otherwise, just log it." Conditions let one workflow handle several cases.

### Where AI fits

AI is useful when the middle of the workflow requires understanding language. Examples:

- **Classify:** is this message a question, a complaint or a compliment?
- **Extract:** pull the date, name and amount out of an email.
- **Summarise:** reduce a long message to two lines.
- **Draft:** write a first reply for you to review.
- **Transform:** convert notes into a table.

Rules-based steps handle the rest, such as moving files, adding rows and sending notifications. Use plain rules wherever rules are enough. They are cheaper, faster and more predictable than AI.

## Choose a good first task

The ideal first automation is repetitive, rule-like, low-stakes and visible. Good candidates:

- Saving attachments from specific emails into a folder.
- Adding form responses to a spreadsheet and sending a thank-you note.
- Creating a weekly reminder with a checklist.
- Sorting incoming messages into labels by topic.
- Producing a draft summary of a document that lands in a shared folder.

Poor first candidates include anything that sends money, deletes data, replies to customers without review, or makes decisions about people.

### Design on paper first

Before opening any tool, write a six-line plan:

```
Task name:
Trigger (what starts it):
Input data (what information arrives):
Steps (numbered, in order):
Output (where results go, who sees them):
Human check (what a person reviews and when):
```

Walk through three imaginary examples, including a messy one with missing information. If you cannot describe what should happen in each case, the workflow is not ready to build.

## Add an AI step with guardrails

When you include an AI step, write its prompt as carefully as you would for a person. Here is a template for a classification step:

```
You will receive a message from a customer. Classify it as exactly one of:
QUESTION, COMPLAINT, REQUEST, OTHER.
Return only the label. If the message is unclear or contains sensitive personal information, return OTHER.
Message: {{message text}}
```

Constraints keep the output predictable. Because the result feeds into later steps, ask for a fixed format, such as one of a few labels or a few labelled lines, rather than free text.

### Keep a person in the loop

Early on, make the workflow produce drafts, not final actions. For example, create a draft reply in your email program instead of sending it, or put a row in a "needs review" sheet. After you have watched the workflow handle dozens of real cases, you may decide that certain narrow actions are safe to automate fully. Keep the risky ones manual.

## Test with sample data

Run your workflow with at least five test inputs: a normal one, one with missing information, one very long, one in unexpected formatting and one that should be ignored. Check each result. Review logs after the first week of real use and fix surprises. Automations break silently when an app changes, a field is renamed or a login expires, so schedule a monthly check.

### Think about privacy and cost

Each connected app gains access to your data, so connect only what the workflow needs and review permissions in each service. Do not pass sensitive personal information through an AI step unless your policy allows it. Many tools limit free usage or charge by volume, so check each provider's official pricing page for current terms, and watch for workflows that run more often than intended.

## Grow gradually

After your first workflow runs well, add one improvement at a time: another condition, a notification, a weekly summary. Document each workflow in a short note describing what it does, why it exists and how to switch it off. That note is a lifesaver when you return months later or hand the workflow to someone else.

### A worked example: a feedback inbox

Say you collect feedback through an online form. The manual routine is to open each response, copy it to a sheet, decide whether it is urgent and write a thank-you note. As an automation, the trigger is "new form response." Step one adds the response to a sheet. Step two sends the text to an AI step that returns one of three labels and a one-line summary. Step three, a condition, checks the label: if it is a complaint, a draft reply is created for you to review and a notification is sent; otherwise the row is simply tagged.

Notice what stays human. The AI never sends anything to the customer. It sorts and drafts. You still read the complaints, and you can spot-check the other labels weekly. If after a month the labels are consistently right, you might automate the thank-you for plain compliments, because the stakes are low. The complaint handling stays manual.

## Questions to ask before you switch anything on

- What is the worst thing that could happen if this step goes wrong?
- Would I notice quickly if it stopped working?
- Can I turn it off in one click?
- Who else is affected by what it sends or changes?
- Does it handle unusual inputs safely, such as empty fields or very long text?

## Common mistakes

- **Automating a broken process.** Fix the process first.
- **Choosing a high-stakes first task.**
- **Letting AI send or delete automatically** without review.
- **Skipping tests with messy data.**
- **Forgetting maintenance.** Connections and formats change.
- **Over-connecting accounts** and granting broad permissions.
- **Using AI where a simple rule would do.**

## Next steps

Create dependable prompts for AI steps with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), find productivity templates at [/prompts/category/productivity](/prompts/category/productivity), and browse more assistants in [/ai-tools](/ai-tools).

faq.q: What is the simplest way to start with automation?
faq.a: Pick one small, repetitive, low-risk task, such as saving email attachments or sorting form responses. Write the steps on paper, then build it in a no-code tool and test with sample data.

faq.q: Do I need to code to automate tasks with AI?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Many no-code tools connect apps with triggers and actions and can include an AI step. Coding helps for custom needs, but beginners can achieve a lot without it.

faq.q: Is it safe to let AI act automatically?
faq.a: Be careful. Start with drafts and suggestions that a person approves, avoid automatic sending or deleting, and keep logs. Increase autonomy only after the workflow proves reliable on low-risk tasks.

faq.q: How do I know what to automate first?
faq.a: Look for tasks you repeat weekly, that follow clear rules and take at least a few minutes each time. Avoid tasks with high stakes, unclear rules or frequent exceptions. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

title: How to Build a Daily AI Workflow for Work or Study
excerpt: Design a realistic daily routine with AI: morning planning, focused work, reviews and a weekly reset, with prompts and boundaries that keep you in control.
seo_title: How to Build a Daily AI Workflow for Work or Study
seo_description: Build a simple daily AI routine: plan your day, delegate drafts, review outputs, protect focus and reset weekly, with prompts you can copy and adapt.
content:
A good daily AI workflow is small: a five-minute morning plan, two or three delegated tasks with clear prompts, a review habit that keeps you responsible for the output, and a weekly reset to remove what is not helping. Aim to save effort on routine work and protect the thinking that matters, rather than trying to use AI for everything.

## Start by auditing your day

Before adding tools, notice where time goes. For three days, jot down tasks that felt repetitive, slow or draining. Sort them into three groups:

- **Delegate:** routine drafting, formatting, summarising, brainstorming lists.
- **Assist:** tasks where AI offers options but you decide, like planning, outlining or feedback.
- **Keep:** high-stakes judgement, sensitive conversations, original thinking and anything requiring accountability.

Only the first two groups belong in your AI routine.

### Morning: a five-minute plan

Write down everything on your mind, then ask an assistant to help organise it:

```
Here are my tasks and commitments for today: [brain dump].
I have [number] hours of focused time, with fixed events at [times].
Group them by urgency and effort, suggest a realistic order, and flag anything that seems too big for one sitting.
Ask me up to three questions if priorities are unclear. Do not add tasks I did not list.
```

Treat the answer as a proposal. You decide the final three priorities for the day. Students can use the same prompt with deadlines and study blocks, and the [study planner](/study-planner) helps turn the plan into a schedule.

## During the day: delegate in small, clear chunks

Keep one browser tab or app ready for quick tasks and use consistent prompts. Typical uses:

- Draft a reply from bullet points.
- Turn rough notes into a clean list.
- Ask for three ways to explain a concept.
- Explain an error or an unfamiliar term.
- Get a second opinion on an outline.

Give each request context, a goal and a format. A prompt of ten extra words often saves a revision round.

### Protect your focus

AI can become a distraction if you keep checking it. Use time blocks. For example, do deep work for forty-five minutes with no assistant open, then spend ten minutes batch-processing small tasks with it. If you notice yourself asking questions you could answer in a minute of thought, close the tab.

## Review every output

Make review a standing habit, not an afterthought. A short checklist:

1. Is it true? Verify facts, numbers and names.
2. Is it mine? Does it match my voice and my intention?
3. Is it safe? No private data exposed, no promises I cannot keep.
4. Is it needed? Could it be shorter or removed?

If you are a student, also check your institution's rules on AI assistance and be open about using it where required.

### Evening: a two-minute capture

At the end of the day, note one thing the assistant helped with and one thing that went poorly. For the successes, save the prompt. For the failures, note what was missing: context, format, constraints, or simply the wrong task for AI. This tiny log is how your workflow improves.

### Weekly reset

Once a week, spend fifteen minutes on a review:

```
Here are my notes on what worked and what did not this week: [paste].
Suggest three changes to my AI routine, based only on these notes.
For each, say what I would stop, start or change, and how I would know it worked.
```

Delete prompts you no longer use. Add new ones to your library. Remove any tool that does not clearly earn its place.

## Set boundaries and habits

- Decide what you will never paste: passwords, private records, confidential client information, other people's personal details.
- Keep important decisions human.
- Take a day or a block regularly to work without AI, to keep skills fresh.
- Cite or disclose AI help where your school or workplace requires it.
- Check official help pages for data and privacy controls, since they change.

### Example routine for a student

Morning: plan the day with deadlines and class times. Midday: ask for an explanation of a hard concept at your level, then try the practice problems yourself. Afternoon: write your own draft of an assignment, then request feedback on structure and clarity without asking for a rewrite. Evening: ask for five self-test questions on the day's material and answer them without notes.

## Example routine for a professional

Morning: prioritise tasks and draft a short standup update. Midday: turn meeting notes into action items. Afternoon: polish one important email and ask for objections your reader might have. Evening: log what worked and update your prompt library.

### Make your prompts reusable

The biggest long-term gain in a daily workflow comes from reuse. Create a note called "My daily prompts" with five to eight entries: a planning prompt, a reply-drafting prompt, a notes-to-actions prompt, an explain-this prompt, a critique-my-draft prompt and a weekly review prompt. Each should have placeholders in square brackets. When you need one, copy, fill in and run it. After a few weeks you will notice which ones you use daily and which you can delete.

Add one line of standing context at the top that you paste when relevant, such as "I am a second-year student writing in plain English; avoid jargon" or "I am a project coordinator; keep emails under 120 words." This gives every conversation the same baseline without retyping.

## Adjust for energy and workload

Your workflow should flex. On a heavy day, shrink it to the morning plan and one delegated task. On a creative day, use the assistant only for feedback after you have drafted something. On a low-energy day, lean on it for formatting and tidying, and keep decisions for later. A routine that survives bad days is better than a perfect one you abandon.

## Common mistakes

- **Using AI for every tiny task.** It becomes friction.
- **Skipping the plan.** Without priorities, AI just helps you do unimportant things faster.
- **Not reviewing outputs.**
- **Letting prompts live in your head.** Save them.
- **Outsourcing learning.** Do your own first attempt.
- **Never pruning.** Keep only what helps.

## Next steps

Pick starting prompts from [/prompts/category/productivity](/prompts/category/productivity), craft your own in the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), and explore options in [/ai-tools](/ai-tools).

faq.q: How much time should I spend using AI each day?
faq.a: There is no ideal number. Use it where it saves effort or improves quality, and stop when it creates distraction. A short planning session and a few targeted tasks are enough for most people.

faq.q: What tasks are best to start with in a daily AI routine?
faq.a: Begin with low-risk, repetitive tasks such as planning your day, drafting routine messages, summarising notes and brainstorming. Keep final judgement, sensitive decisions and fact-checking with you. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: Will relying on AI make me worse at thinking?
faq.a: It can if you outsource everything. Do your own first attempt on important tasks, use AI for feedback and options, and regularly work without it so your core skills stay sharp.

faq.q: Should I keep one long chat or start new ones?
faq.a: Start a new conversation per task or project to keep context clean. Keep a short saved note of reusable instructions, and paste it in when needed rather than relying on one endless thread.

title: 12 Common AI Mistakes to Avoid When Using Chat Assistants
excerpt: Avoid the errors that waste time and cause embarrassment when using AI chat tools: vague prompts, blind trust, privacy slips and over-reliance, with fixes.
seo_title: 12 Common AI Mistakes to Avoid With Chat Tools
seo_description: Learn twelve common mistakes people make with AI chat assistants, from vague prompts and blind trust to privacy slips, and the simple habits that fix each.
content:
The most common AI mistakes are not technical. They are habits: asking vaguely, trusting too quickly, pasting what you should not, and handing over thinking you should keep. Here are twelve, each with a fix you can apply today.

## 1. Writing vague prompts

"Write something about marketing" gets generic output. Fix it by stating the audience, goal, format, length and tone, and by including real details.

```
Write a 150-word intro for a newsletter aimed at small bakery owners about using a simple weekly posting schedule.
Tone: friendly and practical. End with one question to the reader.
```

### 2. Trusting answers without checking

Assistants can state wrong facts fluently. Verify names, dates, numbers, legal or medical statements and anything you will publish. For important claims, find the original source, and when it matters, ask a qualified professional.

### 3. Believing invented sources

Generated citations, quotes and statistics can be fabricated. Search for the source in a trusted database or on the official site. If you cannot find it, do not use it.

## 4. Pasting private or confidential data

Passwords, financial details, health records, client secrets and other people's personal information do not belong in a casual chat. Replace names with roles, remove identifiers, and read the provider's data controls and your workplace policy first.

### 5. Accepting the first answer

The first response is a draft. Ask follow-ups: "Make this shorter," "Give me two alternatives," "What is weak in this argument?" Iterating is where assistants become really useful.

### 6. Giving too many tasks in one prompt

A prompt that asks for research, a plan, a draft and a critique all at once produces shallow results. Break big jobs into steps and check each output before moving on.

### 7. Never providing examples

If you want a certain style or format, show it. Paste a short sample of what good looks like and say "match this structure." Examples beat adjectives.

## 8. Forgetting the assistant cannot see what you see

It does not know your file, your class rubric or your boss's preferences unless you share them. Provide relevant text (if allowed) or describe the situation. Do not assume it remembers earlier chats unless the product clearly offers such a feature and you have checked how it works.

### 9. Using AI where it is not appropriate

Do not submit AI-written work as your own where it is prohibited, rely on it for emergencies, or use it for high-stakes professional advice without expert review. For medical, legal or financial decisions, consult a qualified professional.

### 10. Letting your voice disappear

Heavy reliance on generated text makes writing bland. Write a first draft yourself, or edit generated drafts hard, adding your examples, opinions and phrasing. Readers value a real voice.

## 11. Ignoring bias and gaps

Assistants reflect patterns in their training data, which may contain stereotypes and blind spots. When writing about people, culture or contested topics, ask for multiple perspectives, check for loaded language and review the output with a critical eye.

### 12. Not saving what works

If you craft a great prompt and lose it, you start again. Keep a notes file of prompts that worked, with the task, the date and what to change next time.

### A simple pre-send checklist

Before using any AI output, run through five quick questions:

1. **Accurate?** Facts verified from reliable sources.
2. **Appropriate?** Allowed by rules at your school or workplace.
3. **Private?** No sensitive data exposed.
4. **Authentic?** Edited to reflect your own thinking.
5. **Useful?** Does it actually serve the reader?

This takes under a minute and prevents most embarrassing errors.

### How to recover when something goes wrong

If you discover an AI error after sharing, correct it promptly and plainly. Tell the people who received it, fix the document and note what you will check next time. If you realise you pasted something sensitive, check the tool's data controls, delete the conversation where possible, and inform the right person at your workplace according to policy. Mistakes are normal while learning, and handling them well builds trust.

## Build better habits gradually

Do not try to fix all twelve at once. Pick two this week, for example "state the audience in every prompt" and "verify one fact before sending." Next week, add two more. In a month, these will feel automatic and your results will improve noticeably.

### Examples of fixing a weak prompt

**Before:** "Explain photosynthesis."

**After:** "Explain photosynthesis to a 14-year-old in about 150 words. Use one everyday analogy, define chlorophyll, and end with two quiz questions with answers. Do not use jargon without explaining it."

**Before:** "Write my cover letter."

**After:** "Here is the job advertisement and my CV bullet points. Draft a one-page letter that highlights three relevant achievements, uses a confident but modest tone, and only claims things listed in my bullets. Ask me questions if you need more information."

The second versions give the assistant the audience, the structure, the limits and the facts. They also include a built-in safeguard against invented details. Small changes like these turn mediocre outputs into useful drafts, and they take under a minute to write.

### Signs that you are over-relying on AI

Watch for warning signs: you reach for the assistant before thinking about a problem for even a minute, you cannot explain your own work without it, your writing sounds unlike you, or you feel anxious doing a task alone. None of these are failures, only signals to rebalance. Set aside regular practice time without it, and use it for feedback on your attempts rather than for first drafts of everything.

## Common mistakes

This whole article is about them, but three deserve repeating: trusting without checking, sharing what you should not, and skipping your own thinking. If you fix only those, you avoid most of the serious problems.

## A weekly habit to lock in the lessons

Pick one real output from the week and audit it against this list. Where did you give too little context? Which fact did you not verify? Did you paste anything you would now remove? Write one sentence about what you will do differently and add it to your prompt notes. Ten minutes of honest review each week teaches more than any list of tips, because it uses your own examples and shows which mistakes you personally repeat.

title: How to Fact-Check AI Answers: A Simple Verification Workflow
excerpt: AI can sound sure and be wrong. Use this step-by-step verification routine to sort claims, check sources, catch fake citations and decide what to trust.
seo_title: How to Fact-Check AI Answers Step by Step
seo_description: A practical routine for checking AI answers: split claims, rank risk, trace sources, spot fake citations, cross-check and record what you verified.
content:
To fact-check an AI answer, break it into individual claims, rank them by risk, check the risky ones against reliable original sources, and write down what you confirmed. You do not have to verify every sentence, but you should never publish, submit or act on a claim you have not traced to something solid.

## Why verification is part of the workflow

Chat assistants produce text that sounds right. Sometimes it is right, sometimes it contains small errors, and sometimes it contains complete inventions, such as a study that does not exist or a quote nobody said. The wording is equally confident in all cases, so tone tells you nothing. Verification is not distrust of AI; it is the same discipline you would apply to any unsigned source.

### Step 1: Split the answer into claims

Read the output and highlight each statement that could be true or false: names, dates, numbers, causes, rules, definitions, quotes and references. Ignore opinions and style. A paragraph that seems like one idea may hold six checkable claims.

You can speed this up:

```
List every factual claim in the text below as a numbered list, one per line.
Do not add new claims or judge them. Text: [paste]
```

## Step 2: Rank by risk

Not every claim needs the same effort. Score each as high, medium or low using two questions: how bad is it if this is wrong, and how likely is it to be wrong?

- **High:** numbers, quotes, medical, legal and financial statements, names of real people, anything you will publish or submit.
- **Medium:** background facts you present as true, causal explanations.
- **Low:** widely known basics and brainstorming ideas.

Start with high-risk claims.

### Step 3: Find primary or authoritative sources

For each high-risk claim, look for a source close to the original: an official site, a government or standards body, a textbook, a peer-reviewed article, a company's own documentation. News summaries and blog posts are weaker than the thing they describe. If the claim concerns a product or service, use the provider's official pages, since details change.

Use the search engine, library database or official site yourself. Do not ask the assistant to "provide a link" and trust it without opening the link, because links can be wrong or invented.

### Step 4: Check citations specifically

For any reference the assistant provides:

1. Search the exact title and authors.
2. Confirm the work exists, with the right year and publication.
3. Open it and find the passage that supports the claim.
4. Check that the scope matches: a study of one group does not prove a claim about everyone.

If you cannot find it after a reasonable search, treat it as unreliable and drop it.

## Step 5: Cross-check

Look for at least two independent reliable sources for important claims. "Independent" means they do not just copy each other. If sources disagree, say so in your writing rather than choosing silently, and explain which one you trust and why.

### Step 6: Check numbers and logic

Recalculate figures yourself. Look at units, time periods and whether percentages relate to the right base. If the AI performed a calculation, repeat it with a calculator or spreadsheet. Examine the reasoning: does the conclusion actually follow from the facts?

## Step 7: Record what you verified

Keep a short verification log with the claim, the source you checked and the date. This takes little time and makes it easy to answer questions later or update the content. A simple table works:

| Claim | Risk | Source checked | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example claim | High | Official page | Confirmed, updated wording |

### Prompts that reduce errors in the first place

You cannot remove errors completely, but you can reduce them:

```
Answer using only the text I provide below. If the text does not contain the answer, say "not in the text."
Do not guess. Quote the sentence that supports each point.
```

```
Separate your answer into: (1) things you are confident are well established,
(2) things that depend on context or may have changed, (3) things I should verify and how.
Do not provide links or citations unless I give you the source text.
```

Giving the source and asking for quotes narrows the room for invention. Asking for uncertainty labels is helpful, but the labels are not guarantees.

### Know when to stop and ask a professional

For decisions about health, law, finances, safety or anything with serious consequences, treat AI as a way to prepare questions, not to get answers. Consult a qualified professional, and use official guidance for your country or region.

## Teaching others to verify

If you work with students or a team, make verification visible. Ask for the log, require sources to be opened and read, and discuss examples of errors you caught. Normalising checking prevents embarrassment later and builds good information habits.

### A worked example

Suppose an assistant gives you a paragraph about the history of a public library system, with three dates, one founder's name and a quoted line. You split out the claims and mark the quote and the dates as high risk. You search the library's official history page, which confirms one date, gives a slightly different year for another, and does not mention the founder's name at all. You then check a local archive for the name and find a different spelling. The quote does not appear anywhere you can find, so you remove it.

Result: of six claims, three survive unchanged, two are corrected and one is deleted. Twenty minutes of checking prevented four errors from reaching your readers. The assistant still saved you time, because it gave you a structure and a list of things to check.

## Lateral reading

When you check a source, do not only read it; look sideways. Open a new tab and see who runs the site, what other reliable sources say about it and whether it has a clear way to contact the author or publisher. Professional fact-checkers use this habit because it is faster than judging a site by its design. Apply the same approach to sources an assistant mentions, and to any page that looks authoritative but has no named author or date.

## Common mistakes

- **Equating confident tone with accuracy.**
- **Asking the AI to verify itself** and stopping there.
- **Trusting links without opening them.**
- **Checking only one source.**
- **Ignoring dates.** Information changes, so check how recent a source is.
- **Skipping the quote check.** Misquotes damage credibility.
- **Verifying after publishing** instead of before.

## Next steps

Use research templates from [/prompts/category/students](/prompts/category/students), structure source-bound prompts with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), and see more guides at [/ai-tools](/ai-tools).
