faq.a: Language models generate likely-sounding text rather than looking up verified facts, so they can produce confident errors, including invented sources. This is why checking against reliable originals is essential. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: Can I ask the AI to fact-check itself?
faq.a: It can help flag weak claims or suggest what to verify, but it is not a reliable judge of its own errors. Use it to make a checklist, then confirm each item with independent sources.

faq.q: How do I check if a citation is real?
faq.a: Search the exact title in a library database or publisher site, confirm authors, year and publication, then open the work and check it actually says what is claimed. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: Which claims need the most checking?
faq.a: Numbers, dates, names, quotes, legal, medical and financial statements, and anything you will publish, submit or use to make a decision. Low-stakes brainstorming needs far less checking. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

title: How to Summarize Long Documents With AI Accurately
excerpt: Summarize long reports, articles and contracts with AI by chunking, asking for structure and cross-checking details, so summaries stay accurate and useful.
seo_title: Summarize Long Documents With AI Accurately
seo_description: Learn a reliable method to summarise long documents with AI: define your purpose, chunk the text, request structure, verify details and avoid lost nuance.
content:
Summarising a long document well means telling the assistant why you need the summary, feeding the text in manageable sections, asking for a structured result, and checking the details that matter against the original. A vague "summarise this" often drops the one thing you needed, so purpose and structure make the difference.

## Start with the purpose

A summary for a quick decision differs from a summary for studying. Before you paste anything, answer:

- Who is the reader (you, your manager, a class)?
- What will they do with it (decide, learn, respond, file)?
- What must not be missed (numbers, deadlines, risks, definitions)?
- How long should it be?

Include these answers in your prompt. They guide what counts as important.

### Check permissions and privacy

Documents often contain personal data, client information or unpublished material. Check whether you are allowed to upload or paste them into an AI tool, and read the tool's data controls on its official site. If in doubt, remove names and identifiers, or use only the sections you need.

## Chunk long text

Long documents can overwhelm a single prompt, and details in the middle may get less attention. A reliable method:

1. Split the text by headings, chapters or about a few pages at a time.
2. Summarise each chunk with the same prompt.
3. Paste the chunk summaries together and ask for a combined summary.
4. Check the combined version against the original headings to see if any section vanished.

Using the same prompt for every chunk keeps the format consistent and makes merging easier.

### A prompt for each chunk

```
Summarise the section below for [reader] who needs to [purpose].
Output:
- Main point (one sentence)
- Key facts and figures (bullets, exactly as in the text)
- Decisions, deadlines or actions mentioned
- Terms that need explaining
- Anything that seems unclear or incomplete
Use only the text. Do not add outside information. If the section has nothing relevant, say so.
Section: [paste]
```

Asking for figures "exactly as in the text" reduces rounding or paraphrasing of numbers.

## A prompt for the combined summary

```
Below are summaries of consecutive sections of one document.
Combine them into a [length] summary for [reader]. Start with the single most important takeaway,
then list key points in the order of importance, then open questions.
Keep numbers unchanged. Note any contradictions between sections.
```

### Choose the right summary type

Different jobs need different outputs. Ask explicitly for the one you need:

- **Executive summary:** conclusions and recommendations first.
- **Outline:** headings and sub-points for study.
- **Key points and quotes:** short extracts you can verify.
- **Q&A:** likely questions with answers from the text.
- **Action list:** only tasks, owners and dates.
- **Plain-language version:** the same content in simpler words, flagged where precision matters.

### Verify the parts that matter

Summaries compress, and compression can distort. Check these against the source:

- Numbers, dates and units.
- Names and titles.
- Words like "may," "must," "except" and "unless," which change meaning.
- Negations. "Not required" and "required" are easily swapped.
- Anything you plan to quote or act on.

A useful trick is to ask the assistant for the exact sentence supporting each key point, then search the original for that sentence. If it does not exist, the point is suspect.

## Summarising for study

If you are studying, summarise after you have read, not instead of reading. Try this sequence: read the section, write three sentences in your own words, then ask the assistant to compare your summary with the text and point out missing ideas. Finally, request five questions to test yourself. This keeps your brain in the loop and improves retention far more than reading a polished summary.

### Summarising articles and web pages

For news or opinion pieces, ask for the main claim, the evidence offered, the sources named and the points where the author's perspective shapes the framing. This turns summarising into critical reading and helps you avoid mistaking opinion for fact.

## Keep the original accessible

A summary should point back to the source. Keep page numbers or section titles in the summary so you can return to the full text. If you share a summary with others, say it is a summary and give a way to see the original.

### A worked example: a long project report

You are handed a forty-page project report and a meeting in an hour. Your purpose is to decide whether to approve the next phase. You tell the assistant that the reader is a decision maker who needs risks, costs as stated, deadlines and open issues. You split the report into its six chapters and run the chunk prompt on each. The combined summary leads with the main recommendation, lists the stated costs exactly, and flags that two chapters give different completion dates.

That contradiction is the most useful result. You open both chapters, confirm the discrepancy, and bring it to the meeting as a question. A generic summary might have smoothed it over. Because you specified your purpose and asked for contradictions, the assistant surfaced what mattered.

## Build a summary template you reuse

If you summarise similar documents often, such as weekly reports or journal articles, standardise the output. Decide on five headings and keep them identical each time, for example: purpose, key findings, numbers to remember, risks or limits, next steps. Consistent structure makes it easy to compare documents, spot gaps and share summaries with colleagues who then know where to look.

## Common mistakes

- **No stated purpose.** The summary drops what you needed.
- **Pasting everything at once** and assuming equal attention.
- **Accepting rounded or paraphrased numbers.**
- **Trusting summaries of legal or medical documents** without professional review.
- **Skipping the check for contradictions** between sections.
- **Uploading restricted material** without permission.
- **Replacing reading entirely** when you need to understand deeply.

## Next steps

Find summarising templates in [/prompts/category/education](/prompts/category/education), build your own request in the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), and plan reading sessions with the [study planner](/study-planner).

faq.q: Why does AI miss details in long documents?
faq.a: Very long inputs can exceed limits or lead to uneven attention, so details in the middle may be underweighted. Splitting the document and summarising sections separately improves reliability. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: How long should a summary be?
faq.a: As short as it can be while still serving your purpose. A decision memo might need five bullets, while a study guide needs more. State the target length and the reader in your prompt.

faq.q: Can I summarise a contract or legal document with AI?
faq.a: You can use it to get a plain-language overview, but it can miss or misread clauses. For legal, financial or medical documents, read the original and consult a qualified professional before relying on a summary.

faq.q: Is it okay to upload a confidential document to an AI tool?
faq.a: Only if your organisation allows it and the tool's data handling meets your needs. When unsure, remove sensitive details or summarise from your own notes instead. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

title: Build a Reusable AI Prompt Library and Custom Instructions
excerpt: Stop rewriting prompts from scratch. Learn to organise a personal prompt library, write standing instructions and version your best prompts over time.
seo_title: Build a Reusable AI Prompt Library That Works
seo_description: Create a personal prompt library with templates, placeholders, naming and version notes, plus standing instructions that keep outputs consistent every time.
content:
A prompt library is a small, organised set of prompts you have tested and can reuse by filling in blanks. It turns "I think I wrote something like this last month" into a thirty-second copy and paste, and it keeps quality steady because each prompt carries the context, format and rules that worked before. Start with five prompts for your most frequent tasks and grow only when you need to.

## What belongs in a library

Not every prompt deserves saving. Keep those that meet at least one test:

- You have used something similar three times.
- The result needed several revisions to get right.
- The task has a fixed format, such as a weekly report or a reply type.
- Others on your team might use it.

One-off questions stay out. A bloated library is harder to use than none.

### Anatomy of a reusable prompt

A good template has named parts, so you can fill in and adjust quickly:

```
TITLE: Weekly project update (v3)
USE WHEN: summarising progress for my manager
ROLE: You are a clear, concise project coordinator.
TASK: Turn my notes into a weekly update.
INPUT: [paste notes]
AUDIENCE: [manager name or role], busy, wants decisions and risks first
FORMAT: 1) Headline in one sentence 2) Progress bullets (max 5) 3) Risks 4) Decisions needed
RULES: Use only my notes. Mark gaps as [NEED INFO]. Under 150 words. No filler.
NOTES TO SELF: Works best when I include dates. Add last week's update for comparison.
```

The header lines are for you. The body is what you paste into the assistant. Separating them keeps the library readable.

## Use placeholders consistently

Pick one style, such as square brackets with capital letters: [AUDIENCE], [TOPIC], [PASTE NOTES]. That way you can search for brackets before running a prompt and make sure nothing is unfilled. Leaving a placeholder in a prompt is a common cause of odd outputs.

### Organise so you can find things

Simple structures win. Options include:

1. **By task:** writing, summarising, planning, learning, coding, email.
2. **By project:** each project has its own prompts and background notes.
3. **By frequency:** a "daily" list and a "rare" list.

Use clear titles beginning with a verb: "Summarise meeting into actions," "Explain concept at beginner level," "Critique my draft." Add tags for the tool or subject if you use several.

## Write standing instructions

Standing instructions, sometimes called custom instructions or a system prompt depending on the tool, carry preferences that apply to most of your conversations. Features and wording differ by product and change over time, so check the official help for what yours supports. If it does not support saving them, keep a short block in your library and paste it at the start of a chat.

A starter block:

```
About me: [role, level, field].
How I like answers: plain language, short sentences, lists when useful, no filler praise.
When unsure: say so and ask a question instead of guessing.
Never invent facts, sources, quotes or numbers; mark uncertainty clearly.
For writing tasks: keep my voice, avoid clichés, do not use exaggerated claims.
For learning tasks: explain step by step, then give me a short quiz.
```

Keep it short. Long, contradictory instructions create confusion. Review it every few months.

### Version your prompts

When a prompt improves, do not overwrite silently. Add a version number and a one-line note about what changed and why: "v2: added 'use only my notes' after it invented a deadline." This history teaches you what works and lets you go back if an edit makes things worse.

### Test before you trust

Before adding a prompt to the library, try it on three different inputs, including a messy one. Note where it fails. A prompt that works on your favourite example may break on the second. Add rules for the failures you find, such as "if information is missing, ask me questions first."

## Share carefully

If you share prompts with classmates or colleagues, remove private data, internal names and anything confidential from examples. Add a line explaining when to use the prompt and when not to. A shared prompt with a clear purpose saves everybody time, but a poorly explained one spreads bad habits.

### A starter set of five

1. **Plan my day** from a brain dump.
2. **Turn notes into actions** with owners and dates.
3. **Explain this concept** at my level with an example and a quiz.
4. **Critique my draft** for clarity, structure and tone, without rewriting.
5. **Rewrite for a different audience** while keeping all facts.

These cover a large share of daily needs. Create each one by solving a real task, saving the version that worked and then generalising it.

## Maintenance rhythm

Once a month, spend ten minutes: delete unused prompts, merge near-duplicates, update outdated rules and add one new prompt from a recent success. Note that tools change, so a prompt tuned for one assistant may need adjusting for another. Keep notes on which tool it was tested with.

### A worked example: from messy chat to saved prompt

Suppose you often write polite replies to parents as a teacher. The first time, you write a long prompt, get a draft that is too formal, and refine it over four messages: "warmer," "shorter," "do not promise a meeting," "end with a thank you." Instead of losing all that, copy the final instruction set into your library: role, tone, length, the no-promises rule and the ending. Replace the specific parent and issue with [SITUATION] and [KEY FACTS].

Next time, you paste the template, fill the two blanks and get a near-final draft in one step. You have captured four rounds of learning in one reusable block. After a month you might notice that you always edit the greeting, so you add a rule about it and bump the version to v2. That is how a library improves with use.

## Add a few examples inside the prompt

Examples are the most powerful part of many templates. Include one short sample of the output you want, labelled clearly, such as "Example of the style I like." Keep it brief and free of private data. If a prompt keeps producing the wrong format, an example usually fixes it faster than more rules, because the assistant can imitate the shape you showed.

## Common mistakes

- **Saving everything.** The library becomes clutter.
- **No placeholders.** Prompts get reused with old details.
- **Overlong standing instructions** that conflict with each other.
- **Never updating.** Prompts grow stale.
- **Storing sensitive data** in saved prompts.
- **Copying prompts from the internet unchanged.** Adapt them to your context and test them.

## Next steps

Browse tested starting points in [/prompts](/prompts), build and save structured prompts with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), and see productivity templates at [/prompts/category/productivity](/prompts/category/productivity).

faq.q: What is a prompt library?
faq.a: It is a personal collection of tested prompts with placeholders, notes and examples, stored where you can copy them quickly. It saves time and keeps your results consistent across tasks.

faq.q: Where should I store my prompts?
faq.a: Anywhere you will actually open daily: a notes app, a document, a spreadsheet or a text-expander tool. Choose a simple format, searchable titles and one location so nothing gets scattered.

faq.q: What are custom instructions?
faq.a: Some assistants let you save standing preferences, such as your role, tone and format rules, that apply to chats. Features differ and change, so check the tool's official help for what is available.

faq.q: How many prompts should a library have?
faq.a: Start with five to ten for tasks you repeat weekly. A small library you use beats a large one you forget. Review monthly and delete prompts that no longer earn their place.

title: AI Study Workflow: Learn a New Skill Faster and Responsibly
excerpt: Use AI as a tutor, quiz master and feedback partner to learn any skill. Build a plan, practise actively, test yourself and avoid the illusion of understanding.
seo_title: AI Study Workflow: Learn a New Skill Faster
seo_description: A learning workflow with AI: set a goal, build a plan, explain at your level, practise actively, self-test and review, while keeping effort and honesty central.
content:
The most effective way to learn with AI is to make the assistant do the supporting work, such as explaining, quizzing and giving feedback, while you do the effortful part: attempting, recalling and applying. Learning happens when your brain struggles productively. If the assistant does the struggling, you feel progress without making any.

## Step 1: Define a specific goal

"Learn photography" is too vague. "Take well-exposed portraits in natural light within six weeks" is something you can plan. Write your goal, your current level, how many hours a week you have and how you will know you succeeded. Use this in your prompts as context.

### Step 2: Build a roadmap, then check it

Ask for a plan, and treat it as a draft:

```
I want to [goal]. My current level: [describe]. I can study [hours] per week for [weeks].
Create a roadmap with weekly milestones, a short list of core concepts in a sensible order,
and one practice project per two weeks. Explain why you ordered it this way.
```

Then compare it with a reliable source such as a course syllabus, a textbook's table of contents or advice from an experienced person. Adjust. Plans from assistants can look neat but omit essentials or add unnecessary detail.

## Step 3: Learn concepts at your level

When something is confusing, ask for layered explanations:

```
Explain [concept] in three levels: (1) in two sentences for a 12-year-old,
(2) in a paragraph for a beginner in this field, (3) with a worked example and common misconceptions.
Then ask me one question to check I understood.
```

Answer the check question before reading further. If you cannot, ask for a different explanation or an example from another angle.

### Step 4: Practise actively

Reading is not practising. Convert each concept into something you do:

- Solve problems without looking at solutions.
- Write a short explanation from memory.
- Build a small project using the idea.
- Teach it to a friend or an imaginary student.

When you get stuck, ask for a hint:

```
I am stuck on this problem: [paste]. Here is what I tried: [your attempt].
Give me a hint, not the solution. If I am still stuck, I will ask for a bigger hint.
```

This ladder of hints preserves the struggle that makes memory durable.

## Step 5: Test yourself with spaced retrieval

Ask the assistant to produce practice questions, then answer them from memory, without notes.

```
Create 8 mixed questions on [topic], from easy to hard: some recall, some application.
Do not show answers yet. I will reply with my answers and you will mark them,
explaining any mistakes and telling me which sub-topics to review.
```

Repeat the same topic after a day, a few days and a week. Spaced practice works better than cramming. Keep a list of questions you missed and revisit those first.

### Step 6: Get feedback on your work

For essays, designs, code or speaking practice, use the assistant as a reviewer. Provide your work and criteria:

```
Here is my [essay / design brief / code]. Evaluate it against these criteria: [list or paste rubric].
Give three strengths, three specific improvements and one question to help me think further.
Do not rewrite it.
```

Rewriting your work for you removes the learning. Ask for diagnosis and then do the revision yourself.

### Step 7: Check against trusted material

Assistants can be wrong, especially on specialised or recent topics. Confirm key points in textbooks, official documentation, course notes or expert-reviewed resources. When the assistant and your course disagree, trust the course until you have verified otherwise, and bring the question to your teacher.

## Step 8: Reflect weekly

At the end of each week, write what you learned, what confused you and what you will change. Ask the assistant to propose adjustments to your plan from your notes. A short reflection routine improves your learning more than adding another tool.

### Use AI honestly

Follow school and workplace rules on AI assistance. Use it to understand, practise and improve, not to produce work you present as entirely yours where that is not allowed. If you are unsure, ask. Being open about how you used it protects your learning and your reputation.

## A worked example: learning basic statistics in six weeks

Imagine you want to understand basic statistics for a course. You set a goal, such as interpreting common charts and running simple tests on small datasets, and ask for a roadmap. It proposes six weekly milestones. You compare it with your course syllabus and move one topic earlier. In week one, you ask for the concept of an average explained at three levels, then answer the check question without looking. You solve five practice problems from your textbook before asking for any hints.

On day three you request eight mixed questions and answer them from memory. You miss two, so the assistant marks them and points to the sub-topic. You review, and two days later you try similar questions again. By the end of the week you can explain averages and spread to a friend using your own example. Every stage involved effort from you and support from the assistant, and nothing was copied.

### Build a simple weekly rhythm

A sustainable pattern helps more than occasional long sessions. For example: two short sessions to learn new material, two to practise without help, one to test yourself, and one to review mistakes. Place the most demanding session when you are most alert. Use the assistant mainly in the learn and review sessions, and keep the practice and testing sessions assistant-free until you have attempted everything.

## Pair AI with other resources

Combine the assistant with a textbook or course, a community or study group and real-world practice. Each fills gaps the others leave. A group can challenge your reasoning, a textbook gives vetted explanations and practice gives feedback no explanation can replace. The assistant is the flexible connector between them, able to translate jargon, make quizzes and suggest what to do next.

## Common mistakes

- **Passive reading of explanations.** Feeling that you understand is not the same as being able to do it.
- **Asking for solutions immediately.**
- **Trusting the roadmap without checking.**
- **Skipping spaced review.**
- **Using AI to write assignments** where that is not allowed.
- **Switching topics constantly.** Depth beats variety at the start.
- **Neglecting rest and breaks.** Memory consolidates over time.

## Next steps

Plan sessions with the [study planner](/study-planner), find learning templates in [/prompts/category/students](/prompts/category/students), and explore more options in [/ai-tools](/ai-tools).

faq.q: Can AI replace a teacher or tutor?
faq.a: It can supplement one by explaining, quizzing and giving feedback, but it can also be wrong and cannot fully judge your progress. Use it with reliable course materials and, where possible, human guidance.

faq.q: How do I avoid just copying answers from AI?
faq.a: Attempt problems first, ask for hints before solutions, and explain answers in your own words. If you could not reproduce the solution tomorrow without help, you have not learned it yet.

faq.q: What is active recall and how does AI help?
faq.a: Active recall means retrieving information from memory instead of rereading. AI can generate practice questions and check your answers, but you must answer from memory before looking at the explanations.

faq.q: Is using AI for homework allowed?
faq.a: Rules vary by school and course. Check your teacher's or institution's policy, use AI only in permitted ways, and be honest about assistance. Never submit generated work as your own where that is prohibited.

title: What Not to Paste Into AI Chatbots: A Privacy-Safe Workflow
excerpt: Protect yourself and others when using AI chat tools. Learn what to keep out of prompts, how to anonymise text, check data settings and build safe habits.
seo_title: What Not to Paste Into AI Chatbots: Safe Workflow
seo_description: A practical privacy guide for AI chat tools: what to never paste, how to anonymise data, how to check settings and policies, and a quick pre-paste checklist.
tags: what not to share with chatgpt
content:
The safe default is simple: if you would not post it publicly or hand it to a stranger, do not paste it into a chatbot unless you have checked the tool's data rules and have permission. Anonymise first, share the minimum needed, and read the provider's official privacy settings, because policies and controls differ and change over time.

## Why this matters

When you type into an online tool, your text travels to a service run by a company. What happens next depends on that company's policies, your account type and settings, and the agreements your school or employer has with it. Some services may store conversations, allow staff review in certain cases, or use content to improve products unless you change a setting. You cannot know this from memory, so the official privacy policy and settings pages are the source of truth.

Privacy is also about other people. Pasting a friend's message, a student's work or a client's details shares their information without their say.

### What to keep out of prompts

As a rule, avoid pasting:

- **Credentials:** passwords, API keys, security codes, recovery phrases.
- **Financial details:** card numbers, bank accounts, tax documents.
- **Government identifiers** and similar official numbers.
- **Health information** about yourself or others.
- **Confidential work material:** unreleased plans, contracts, client lists, source code covered by agreements.
- **Personal data about others:** full names with contact details, addresses, student records, HR matters.
- **Private messages** where others have not agreed to share them.
- **Exam or assessment material** that you are not permitted to share.

If a task seems to require such data, look for a way to do it with placeholders or a smaller sample.

## The anonymise-and-restore method

Most tasks do not need real identifiers. Use this routine:

1. Copy the text into a scratch note.
2. Replace names with roles or labels: [MANAGER], [CLIENT A], [STUDENT 1].
3. Remove or generalise contact details, locations and account numbers.
4. Check for details that could still identify someone, such as a unique job title or a rare event.
5. Paste the cleaned version into the assistant.
6. When you get the result, restore the real details yourself.

Example before and after:

```
Before: "Priya at Northwind Ltd asked for a refund of the invoice dated 3 May."
After: "[CLIENT CONTACT] at [COMPANY] asked for a refund of an invoice from last month."
```

### Check settings and policies

Before relying on any tool, spend ten minutes finding answers to these questions on its official site:

- Are conversations saved, and for how long?
- Can I turn off history or the use of my content for improving the product?
- Can I delete conversations or my account, and what does deletion cover?
- Who can access my content, and under what circumstances?
- Are there different terms for personal, school and business accounts?
- Where can I report a problem?

Write down what you find and revisit it occasionally, since policies are updated.

## Know your organisation's rules

Many schools and workplaces have AI policies. They may list approved tools, ban uploads of certain content or require disclosure of AI use. If a policy exists, follow it. If none exists, ask a manager, teacher or IT team before using AI with anything sensitive. Using an unapproved tool for confidential material can create real problems even when you meant well.

### Be careful with files, images and screenshots

Documents and screenshots often contain hidden details: names in headers, metadata, other tabs, notifications and email addresses. Before uploading, crop screenshots, remove metadata where you can and view the whole file. Photos can reveal locations and faces. If you are sharing images of people, especially children, get permission and consider whether the task needs the image at all.

## Protect the output too

AI results can include inaccurate or sensitive details you gave it, and saved chats may be visible to others who use your device or account. Use strong passwords and two-step verification on your accounts, log out on shared computers and avoid screenshots of sensitive chats in public channels.

### Create a pre-paste checklist

Keep this note by your keyboard:

1. Do I have permission to share this?
2. Does it contain anything sensitive or identifying?
3. Can I get the same help with placeholders?
4. Have I checked this tool's data settings?
5. Would I be comfortable if this text were seen by the person it concerns?

If any answer worries you, stop and adjust.

## A worked example: asking for help with a difficult email

Suppose you want help replying to a complaint from a customer. The original email includes their full name, address, order number and a description of a medical issue. Pasting it as is would share all of that. Instead, you write a short summary yourself: "A customer says an item arrived damaged and is asking for a refund. They are upset and mention the delay. Our policy allows refunds within thirty days. I want a calm, helpful reply." The assistant drafts a reply using only that. You add the real name and order number afterwards.

You received the same help, with none of the personal details shared. Summarising in your own words also forced you to think about what matters, which usually improves the final reply.

### For teachers, managers and parents

If you are responsible for other people's information, the standard is higher. Teachers should avoid pasting student names, grades or work into tools that the school has not approved, and should use anonymised examples. Managers should keep performance, health and disciplinary matters out of general AI tools. Parents should think carefully before uploading photos or details of children, and should check the age rules and settings of any service a child uses.

## Plan for a mistake

Everyone slips occasionally. If you realise you pasted something you should not have, stop and note what was shared. Check the tool's settings to delete the conversation and see whether any options apply to your account. If it involved a workplace, school or another person's data, tell the appropriate contact promptly, following the relevant policy. Changing any exposed passwords immediately is sensible. Acting quickly and honestly limits harm and builds trust.

## Common mistakes

- **Assuming a chat is private by default.**
- **Pasting entire emails** with signatures and contact details.
- **Uploading screenshots** without cropping.
- **Forgetting about other people's data.**
- **Never reading the policy** or the settings page.
- **Using personal accounts for work material** against policy.
- **Sharing passwords** to get "help" with a login problem.

## Next steps

Learn to write prompts that need less private detail with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), browse safe starting templates in [/prompts](/prompts), and compare tool options in [/ai-tools](/ai-tools).

faq.q: Is it safe to put personal information into an AI chatbot?
faq.a: It depends on the tool, its settings and your rules, so be cautious. Avoid sensitive personal data unless you have read the provider's data policy and have permission, and prefer anonymised examples.

faq.q: How can I anonymise text before pasting it?
faq.a: Replace names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, account numbers and company names with placeholders like [PERSON A], [CLIENT] or [ACCOUNT]. Remove unusual details that could identify someone, then re-insert real details yourself afterwards.

faq.q: Can I use AI tools with confidential work documents?
faq.a: Only if your employer or school allows it and the tool meets their security requirements. Check your policy first, and when in doubt ask your IT or compliance team before pasting anything.

faq.q: Do deleted chats disappear completely?
faq.a: Retention and deletion practices differ between providers and settings, and they change. Read the official privacy policy and data controls for your tool rather than assuming deleted means gone everywhere.

title: Prompt Chaining: Break Big AI Tasks Into Reliable Steps
excerpt: Get better results on complex jobs by splitting them into a chain of small prompts: plan, draft, critique, revise and check, with templates for each step.
seo_title: Prompt Chaining: Break Big Tasks Into AI Steps
seo_description: Learn prompt chaining: split complex work into plan, draft, critique, revise and verify steps, with copyable prompts and tips for staying in control.
content:
Prompt chaining means doing a big job as a short sequence of focused prompts, reviewing each output before you feed it into the next step. A common chain is plan, draft, critique, revise, check. It works because each step has one clear job, you can correct course early, and you stay in charge of the decisions.

## Why one giant prompt often disappoints

A single prompt such as "research, outline, write and polish a 1,500-word report with sources" asks the assistant to juggle many things at once. Errors in early choices are hidden inside the final result, and it is hard to tell where it went wrong. Chaining exposes each stage so you can fix the plan before the draft, and the draft before the polish.

### The five-step chain

### Step 1: Clarify

Have the assistant ask you questions first. This surfaces missing information before work begins.

```
I want to [task]. Before you start, ask me up to five questions about audience, purpose, constraints and material I have.
Do not produce anything yet.
```

Answer in a few lines.

### Step 2: Plan

```
Based on my answers, propose an outline with section titles and one sentence on what each section will say.
Note what evidence or examples each section needs from me. Do not write the full text yet.
```

Edit the plan. Reorder, cut and add. This is the cheapest place to improve the result.

### Step 3: Draft

```
Write section 1 only, following the approved outline.
Use my notes below and nothing else for facts. Mark gaps as [NEED INFO]. Target 200 words.
```

Drafting section by section keeps quality high and lets you adjust tone early. After the first section, you can say, "More concrete; shorter sentences," and the rest follows that style.

### Step 4: Critique

Ask for a review before you ask for improvements:

```
Review the draft as a sceptical editor. List: unclear passages, unsupported claims, repeated ideas,
places where the tone slips and anything missing from the outline. Be specific and quote the lines. Do not rewrite.
```

For a more independent critique, paste the draft into a new conversation or a different assistant.

### Step 5: Revise and check

```
Revise the draft addressing the points I approved: [list your selections]. Keep everything else unchanged.
Then list any factual claims in the revised text that I should verify.
```

You then verify those claims yourself, using reliable sources.

## Pass information forward deliberately

Each step depends on what you carry forward. Put the key parts into the next prompt explicitly: the approved outline, the style notes and the facts. In a long chat, earlier details can fade or get muddled, so a brief recap such as "Here is the final outline and the rules again" helps. If you start a new conversation, paste only what is needed and remove irrelevant clutter.

## Use "gates" between steps

A gate is a quick human check that must pass before you continue:

- After clarifying: do the answers capture my real goal?
- After planning: would I be happy with this structure?
- After drafting: are all facts from my notes?
- After critique: which points do I actually agree with?
- After revising: is it accurate, appropriate and in my voice?

Gates prevent errors from compounding. They are also where your judgement shows, which is the point of using AI as an assistant rather than a replacement.

### Other useful chains

- **Learning chain:** explain, give an example, quiz me, mark my answers, summarise what I missed.
- **Email chain:** list the key facts, draft, shorten, tone check.
- **Data cleanup chain:** describe the columns, propose cleaning rules, write formulas, test on sample rows.
- **Research reading chain:** preview, glossary, extract, critique, personal summary.
- **Presentation chain:** message, outline, slide text, speaker notes, tough questions.

## When chaining is overkill

Short, simple tasks need only one good prompt. Chaining adds overhead, so reserve it for jobs where mistakes are costly, the output is long or the path is unclear. If you find yourself running the same chain often, save it in your prompt library or consider building it into an automation with a human approval step.

## Chains in automated workflows

If you turn a chain into an automatic workflow, keep each step's output format strict, validate it before moving on and log results. Do not let a chain take irreversible actions without review. Test with messy inputs, and keep a manual path available for when something breaks.

### A worked example: a two-page proposal

You need a two-page proposal for a community garden. In the clarify step, the assistant asks about audience, budget range and what you can offer. You answer in a few lines. In the plan step, it suggests five sections, and you remove one and add a section about volunteers. You then draft the sections one by one using your notes, marking missing figures as [NEED INFO]. In the critique step, a fresh conversation points out that the benefits section repeats the introduction and that a claim about local interest has no source. You decide to cut the repetition and to collect real survey results before keeping the claim.

The final revision is yours in every important way: the structure was your decision, the facts came from your notes and the critique was acted upon selectively. The chain simply made each of those moves clearer and quicker.

## Save chains as checklists

Once a chain works, write it as a numbered checklist with the prompt for each step and the gate question that follows. Store it in your prompt library. Next time you face a similar task, you will not have to reinvent the process, and you will remember to stop for the checks that matter. For routine, low-risk tasks you can later consider moving it into an automation, keeping a human approval step where mistakes would be costly.

## Common mistakes

- **Skipping the plan** and polishing a weak structure.
- **Letting the assistant make decisions** that belong to you.
- **Carrying errors forward** because you did not check between steps.
- **Overlong chains** for simple tasks.
- **Forgetting to restate rules** in later prompts.
- **Asking for critique and rewrite at once.** Separate diagnosis from repair.

## Next steps

Create step prompts with the [Prompt Builder](/prompt-builder), find structured templates in [/prompts/category/writing](/prompts/category/writing), and see more guides at [/ai-tools](/ai-tools).

faq.q: What is prompt chaining?
faq.a: It means splitting a complex task into a sequence of smaller prompts, where each output feeds the next. This usually gives clearer, more controllable results than one giant request. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: Is prompt chaining the same as automation?
faq.a: Not exactly. You can chain prompts manually in a chat, reviewing each step yourself. Automation tools can run chains without you, which is useful for routine jobs but needs testing and safeguards.

faq.q: How many steps should a chain have?
faq.a: As few as needed. Three to five steps is common: plan, draft, critique, revise and check. More steps add effort, so add them only when they clearly improve the result.

faq.q: Should I use the same chat for all steps?
faq.a: Often yes, so the assistant keeps context, but start fresh for unrelated tasks. For a critique step, a new conversation can give a more independent review of the draft. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

title: An AI Job Search Workflow: Resume, Letters and Interviews
excerpt: Use AI to organise your job search without sounding generic: analyse job posts, tailor honest resume bullets, draft letters and rehearse interviews.
seo_title: AI Job Search Workflow: Resume to Interview
seo_description: A practical job search workflow with AI: decode job posts, tailor truthful resume bullets, draft cover letters, practise interviews and track applications.
content:
A strong AI-assisted job search uses the assistant to analyse, organise and rehearse, while every claim in your resume and letters stays true and in your own voice. Treat AI like a coach who helps you see what the employer is asking for, not a ghostwriter who invents a better candidate.

## Step 1: Decode the job post

Paste the public job description and ask for a structured breakdown:

```
Here is a job description. Extract: (1) the five most important responsibilities,
(2) required vs nice-to-have skills, (3) keywords the employer repeats,
(4) the likely top three problems this role must solve, (5) questions I should ask the employer.
Use only the text provided.
```

This reveals what the employer cares about. Highlight where your real experience matches and where it does not.

### Step 2: Build your evidence bank

Before tailoring anything, write a master document of your genuine experience: roles, projects, results, tools, responsibilities, training and achievements, with numbers only when you can support them. Include small stories using the situation, task, action and result pattern. This document is your source of truth. Everything the assistant produces must come from it.

## Step 3: Tailor resume bullets honestly

Give the assistant a job description and a bullet from your evidence bank, and ask for clearer wording, not new facts:

```
Rewrite this resume bullet to be concise and results-focused, starting with a strong verb.
Keep every fact and number exactly as written. Do not add tools, results or responsibilities.
Original: [bullet]. Relevant requirement from the job post: [requirement].
Give three versions.
```

Choose the one that sounds like you. Read each line critically and ask, "Could I explain this in an interview with examples?" If not, remove it. Build the final document in the [resume builder](/resume-builder) and run it through the [ATS resume checker](/ats-resume-checker) to look for formatting and keyword issues.

### Step 4: Draft a cover letter that sounds like a person

Use the assistant for structure and clarity, not for a template everyone else also uses.

```
Draft a one-page cover letter for [role] at [company].
Structure: a specific opening about why this role, two achievements from my notes that match the job,
a short closing with a next step. Tone: warm, direct, modest. No clichés. Use only my notes.
My notes: [paste evidence].
```

Then edit heavily: add why this particular organisation interests you, using details you researched yourself. The [cover letter builder](/cover-letter-builder) can help with layout and polish.

## Step 5: Research the employer

Use the assistant to create a research checklist, then do the research yourself on the employer's official website, public reports and reliable news. Ask for questions to guide your reading rather than for facts about the company, since assistants may be out of date or wrong about specific organisations. Write three observations that connect their needs to your experience.

### Step 6: Practise interviews actively

```
Act as an interviewer for [role]. Ask me one question at a time, mixing behavioural,
situational and role-specific questions. After each answer, give feedback on structure, clarity and specifics,
and suggest one improvement. Do not give me a model answer until I ask.
```

Answer out loud and, if you can, record yourself. Then refine your stories. Practise with a friend or mentor as well. AI practice is helpful, but a real person reacts in ways a script cannot.

### Step 7: Track applications

Create a simple table with columns for company, role, date applied, version of resume used, contact, status and next action. Ask the assistant to help you design reminders for follow-ups, such as a polite message one week after applying, but keep the tracker yourself.

```
Write a short, polite follow-up email for an application sent a week ago for [role].
Mention one specific reason I am interested and offer to provide more information. Under 80 words.
```

## Step 8: Handle rejection and feedback

If you receive feedback, paste the relevant parts, without personal details, and ask for patterns across several applications. Use it to adjust your evidence bank and practice, not to criticise yourself.

### Follow rules and stay honest

Some employers state rules about AI-written applications or assessments. Follow them. Never fabricate qualifications, dates, titles or references. Misrepresentation can end an offer or a career. Protect your personal data: avoid pasting ID numbers, full addresses or private details, and check any tool's data settings first.

## A worked example: tailoring one bullet

Your master document says: "Organised weekly volunteer schedule for 40 people at a local food bank; reduced missed shifts by switching to a shared calendar and reminder messages." The job post asks for coordination skills and clear communication. You ask the assistant to tighten the bullet while keeping facts unchanged. It offers three versions. One adds "increased efficiency by 50%", a number you never gave. You reject it, choose a version that keeps your real facts and verify that the shared calendar and reminders are accurately described. In the interview you can now talk about how you did it, what went wrong and what you learned.

That is the standard: better wording, same truth. If the assistant ever offers an impressive detail you cannot back up, remove it.

### Keep a story bank for interviews

Prepare six to eight short stories from your evidence bank covering teamwork, a mistake and what you learned, a time you led something, a problem you solved, a deadline you handled and a time you received feedback. Write each in a few lines with the situation, your actions and the result. Practise adapting them to different questions. The assistant can quiz you and comment on clarity, but the stories must come from your real life.

## Salary and offers

When you reach the offer stage, use AI to prepare questions and to organise your thoughts, not to decide for you. Find reliable local information from official sources and professional advisers where needed. Be cautious with any numbers an assistant provides about pay, since they may be outdated or inaccurate. Make decisions based on verified information and your own priorities.

## Common mistakes

- **Letting AI invent achievements.**
- **Submitting generic letters** with no company-specific detail.
- **Keyword stuffing.** Add terms only where you truly have the skill.
- **Skipping interview practice** out loud.
- **Trusting AI facts about a company** without checking.
- **Using one resume for every job.**
- **Ignoring application instructions.**

## Next steps

Create your document with the [resume builder](/resume-builder), compare layouts at [/resume-templates](/resume-templates), and find prompts in [/prompts/category/careers](/prompts/category/careers).

faq.q: Can I use AI to write my resume?
faq.a: You can use it to draft and polish wording, but every line must be true and yours. Provide real achievements, edit the output, and be ready to explain every claim in an interview.

faq.q: Will employers know my application was written with AI?
faq.a: Generic, buzzword-heavy text can look machine-written. Add specific details, real numbers you can support and your own voice. Follow any employer instructions about AI use in applications. Check official guidance and your own rules for current details.

faq.q: How can AI help me prepare for interviews?
faq.a: It can ask practice questions, give feedback on your structure and help you shape stories, but it cannot predict what a specific interviewer will ask. Practise answering aloud in your own words.

faq.q: Should I paste a whole job description into AI?
faq.a: Job descriptions are usually public, so it is generally fine. Avoid pasting private personal data such as full contact details, and keep your own resume anonymised if the tool's data rules concern you.
